articleTitle: Information management in support of the business
abstract: The introduction of new methods to improve the recording, communication, processing, evaluation and security of information, the increasing availability of cheap computing power and improvements in global communication facilities have promised much. However, in many cases actual achievements have fallen far short of the expectation. In contrast, there have been some cases of spectacular success. Does this mean that success in this field is a hit and miss affair, or are there some lessons to be learned that can help to engineer effective low cost information systems that can respond rapidly to change? The paper aims to provide a positive response to this question. It presents a number of case histories which highlight some of the drawbacks of conventional methods. It traces the formulation of a strategy for the successful development and implementation of effective low cost enterprise wide information systems and business processes that can respond rapidly to change. This strategy is based on the adoption of a holistic approach and the use of mixed methods. Both these basic principles can be easily applied within the framework of two complementary methodologies called Simple Architectures and Models (SAM) and Mixed Open Methods (MOM). SAM and MOM are the results of many years of experience in helping organisations in the commercial environment to successfully manage the implementation of business process reengineering (BPR) programmes and enterprise wide information systems within short timescales.

articleTitle: Data management in support of an integrated information policy: an Army perspective
abstract: The Army (in the UK) has a long term goal of providing a federation of interoperable systems so as to give the users the impression of "a single and fully integrated Army CIS for use in peace and war, on and off the battlefield, by the year 2010". Effective data management is seen as essential if interoperability is to be achieved. We identified that the way to achieve effective data management was to build a single logical data model for the whole of the Army, with the model being built by projects collaborating with the data management organisation to expand a central core. This central core is based on the requirements of the staff of an operational headquarters. The major problem to be overcome in a collaborative exercise of this kind is the data modeller's natural inclination to demonstrate his artistry by producing his model without benefit of previous work. This implies that it is necessary to effect a change in the prevailing culture within the data modelling community. Those of us involved in data management in the Army believe that this culture change can be achieved. The wider exposure of our model to an ever growing number of analysts, each coming from a different viewpoint, can only serve to enrich our model and at the same time, increase the understanding of our purpose so as to reduce the problems to be overcome.

articleTitle: Information Management In NatWest UK Human Resources
The chicken and egg syndrome: business process re-design (BPR) and data management
abstract: The paper examines the relationship between business process redesign (BPR) and data management. It describes the BPR philosophy, the balanced relationship it has with data management and the different implementation approaches possible. It concludes that both are valuable when improving business performance, but greater benefits can be achieved through their synergy. Both approaches have evolved so that the best method depends on the business's current position and objectives and both can be successful.

articleTitle: Engineering information management in London Underground Limited
abstract: London Underground Limited has taken a proactive stance in realizing the need for a company engineering information management system. Two main cultural changes have ban instrumental in bringing information management to the forefront; namely, the adoption of a system/process approach to engineering management and the introduction and escalation of numerous IT 'solutions'. The paper intends to outline the approach taken by London Underground in establishing an engineering information management system within the new culture.
